lines.text: Perception is a best guess.
Here's a checkerboard, with a cylinder standing on it.
The cylinder casts a shadow across the board.
Look at the two squares marked A and B.
Which one is lighter?
Decide before we go on.
Most people say B.
It looks much lighter than A.
Now let's cover everything except the two squares.
Without the board and the shadow, A and B look the same.
Because they are the same.
Exactly the same grey.
Bring the scene back, and join the squares with a bar of that same grey.
Follow the bar from A to B.
There's no edge where the colour changes.
Even now that you know, B probably still looks lighter.
Knowing the answer doesn't switch the effect off.
The same amount of light reaches your eye from both squares.
But your brain sees that B is in shadow.
So it infers that B is a light square in dim light, and A is a dark square in bright light.
It reports what the surfaces are probably like, not how much light reaches your eye.
That's perception.
A best guess, built from context, and from what usually happens in the world.
Usually, it's a very good guess.
Your students make guesses like this whenever they look at a new diagram or graph.
You already know what matters.
Their eyes are still guessing.
So tell them what to look at.
Based on Edward Adelson's checker-shadow illusion, from 1995.
